                  <ns0:head>CHAP. XLIV.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 AND he commanded the <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> him that was over his house.</ns0:note> Steward of his house, saying, Fill the mens sacks <ns0:hi>with</ns0:hi> food, as much as they can carry, and put every mans money in his sacks mouth.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 And put my cup <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">It seems to have been a large cup and of great price and much used by <ns0:hi>Ioseph.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, the silver cup, in the sacks mouth of the youngest <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">With design to discover their intentions and affections towards <ns0:hi>Benjamin,</ns0:hi> whether they did envy him and would desert him in his danger, as they did <ns0:hi>Ioseph;</ns0:hi> or would cleave to him, that hence he might take his measures how to deal with him and them.</ns0:note>, and his corn-money: and he did according to the word that Joseph had spoken.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 As soon as the morning was light, the men were sent away, they, and their asses.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 And when they were gone out of the city, and not <ns0:hi>yet</ns0:hi> far off, Joseph said unto his Steward, Up, follow after the men: and when thou dost over<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />take them, say unto them, Wherefore have ye re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />warded evil for good?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 Is not this it in which my lord drinketh? and whereby indeed he <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> maketh trial.</ns0:note> divineth <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Amongst the several kinds of divination in use among the <ns0:hi>Egyptians</ns0:hi> and other Heathens, this was one to do it by a cup or bason, which they filled with water and put in them plates of silver or precious stones in which certain characters were in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />graven, by which and some words they used they called upon the Devil, who gave them answer. <ns0:hi>Ioseph</ns0:hi> did not use this course nor was a diviner, but the people thought him such an one, and the Steward might represent him as such for the bet<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter covering or carrying on his design. But this sence agrees not with the 15th. verse of this chapter, <ns0:hi>Wot you not,</ns0:hi> &c. Which words shew that he speaks of something which they all might easily know<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> but they did not know that <ns0:hi>Ioseph</ns0:hi> was a Diviner, much less that he divined by that cup, whereas that kind of divination was generally performed by a glass, not by a cup. Others observe, that the Hebrew word ofttimes signifies not to <ns0:hi>divine,</ns0:hi> but onely to <ns0:hi>observe</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>discover</ns0:hi> a thing, as <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 30. 27. 1 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 20. 33. and render the place thus, <ns0:hi>whereby he will cer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tainly observe</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>discover,</ns0:hi> to wit, what you are and do. But this also seems not to consist with <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 15. and the supplement is too large and remote. The true sense then is this, the Hebrew, <ns0:hi>bo,</ns0:hi> is not to be rendered, <ns0:hi>by which,</ns0:hi> but, <ns0:hi>concerning which,</ns0:hi> as the particle <ns0:hi>b<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>th</ns0:hi> is oft used, and it notes not the instrument whereby, but the object about which, he did divine, and the words must be rendred, <ns0:hi>concerning which he can or would certain<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly divine.</ns0:hi> And this agrees well with <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 15. q. d. did you think you could deceive my Master! did not you and all others know that he could divine and discover secret things, whence he had both his name and preferment! And this cup being much prized and used by him, you might easily judge that he would use his art to recover it.</ns0:note>? ye have done evil <ns0:note n="*" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) Very evil, unjust<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly, unthankfully and foolishly.</ns0:note> in so doing.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:42" />6 And he overtook them, and he spake unto them these same words.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 And they said unto him, wherefore saith my Lord these words? God forbid that thy servants should do according to this thing.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 Behold, the money which we found in our sacks mouths, we brought again unto thee out of the land of Canaan: how then should we steal out of thy Lords house silver or gold <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">It is not probable that we who restored that which was in our power to keep and to conceal without any danger should steal that which was likely to be discovered with so much shame and hazard to our selves.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 With whom <ns0:hi>soever</ns0:hi> of thy servants it be found, both <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 31. 32.</ns0:note> let him die, and we also will be my Lords bondmen <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">This over-daring offer proceeded from hence that they were all conscious of their own innocency, and did not suspect any fraud or artifice in the matter.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 And he said, Now also let it be according unto your words: he with whom it is found, shall be my servant, and ye shall be blameless <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Thus he moderates the conditions which they proposed, ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />empting the innocent, and exchanging the deserved and offered death of the nocent into slavery.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 Then they speedily took down every man his sack to the ground, and opened every man his sack.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 And he searched, and began at the eldest <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">To take off all their suspicion of his fraud.</ns0:note> and left at the youngest: and the cup <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">He found doubtless the money there, but he accused them not about that matter, both because they had an answer ready to that charge from his own mouth, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 43. 23. and because the greater crime, the stealing of the cup which <ns0:hi>Ioseph</ns0:hi> so much prized and used, might seem to extinguish the less, or at least cause him to neglect it.</ns0:note> was found in Benjamins sack.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 Then they rent their clothes, and laded e<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />very man his asse, and returned to the City <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Being afraid and ashamed to go to their father without <ns0:hi>Benjamin,</ns0:hi> concerning whom they had received so severe a charge, and made such solemn promises and imprecations.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 And Judah and his brethren came to Josephs house: (for he was yet there) and they fell before him on the ground.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 And Joseph said unto them, What deed is this that ye have done? wot ye not that such a man as I can certainly <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> make trial.</ns0:note> divine?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 And Judah <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Who speaks in the cause, as being one of the eldest, and a person of most gravity and discretion and readiness of speech, and most eminently concerned for his brother.</ns0:note> said, What shall we say unto my Lord? what shall we speak? or how shall we clear our selves? God hath found out the iniquity <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> This ini<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quity, of which it seems some of us are guilty, and God hath discovered it. Or, <ns0:hi>iniquity</ns0:hi> may be put for <ns0:hi>iniquities,</ns0:hi> whether we are guilty of this fact or not we are certainly guilty of many other sins, for which God is now punishing us, to whose provi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dence we therefore willingly submit.</ns0:note> of thy servants: behold, we are my Lords ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vants, both we, and he also with whom the cup is found.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 And he said, God forbid that I should do so: <ns0:hi>but</ns0:hi> the man in whose hand the cup is found, he shall be my servant: and as for you, get you up in peace unto your father.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 Then Judah came near unto him <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Made a little nearer approach to him, that he might pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sent his humble petiti<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> to him.</ns0:note>, and said, O my Lord, let thy servant, I pray thee, speak a word in my Lords ears <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">In thy hearing: For this phrase doth not necessarily imply that he whispered in his ears, as appears from <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 14. 28. <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 32. 44. <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 17. 2.</ns0:note>, and let not thy anger burn against thy servant: for thou art even as Pharaoh <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">As thou representest his person, so thou art invested with his Majesty and Authority, and therefore thy word is a law, thou canst do with us what thou pleasest, either spare or pu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nish us, and therefore we do justly deprecate thine anger and most humbly intreat thy favourable audience and princely com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />passion to us.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 My Lord asked his servants, saying, have ye a father, or a brother?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20 And we said unto ray Lord, we have a father, an old man, and a child of his old age, a little one <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">So they call him comparatively to themselves who were much elder; and withal to signifie the reason why he came not with them because he was young and tender and unfit for such a journey.</ns0:note>, and his brother is dead, and he alone is left of his mother, and his father loveth him.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 And thou saidest unto thy servants, Bring him down unto me, that I may set mine eyes upon him <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) See him with my own eyes, and thereby be satisfied of the truth of what you say. Compare <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 42. 15, 16. Elsewhere this phrase signifies to <ns0:hi>shew favour</ns0:hi> to a person, as <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 39. 12. and 40. 4. But though that was <ns0:hi>Iosephs</ns0:hi> intention, as yet he was minded to conceal it from them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22 And we said unto my Lord, The lad cannot leave his father: for <ns0:hi>if</ns0:hi> he should leave his father, <ns0:hi>his father</ns0:hi> would die.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23 And thou saidest unto thy servants,<ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 43. 3.</ns0:note> except your youngest brother come down with you, you shall see my face no more <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Quest.</ns0:hi> Why would <ns0:hi>Ioseph</ns0:hi> expose his father to the hazard of his life in parting with his dear child! <ns0:hi>Answ. Ioseph</ns0:hi> supposed that to be but a pretence, and might fear lest his brethren had disposed of <ns0:hi>Benjamin,</ns0:hi> as they did of him, and therefore could not bring him forth. And as for his father, the experience which he had of his continuance in life and health after the supposed untimely death of <ns0:hi>Ioseph</ns0:hi> gave him good assurance, that his parting with <ns0:hi>Benjamin</ns0:hi> for a season and that under the care and charge of his brethren was not likely to make any dangerous impression upon him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24 And it came to pass when we came up unto thy servant my father, we told him the words of my Lord.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">25 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 43. 2.</ns0:note> our father said, Go again, and buy us a little food.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26 And we said, we cannot go down: if our youngest brother be with us, then will we go down: for we may not see the mans face, except our youngest brother be with us.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="27">27 And thy servant my father said unto us, Ye know that my wife <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">He calleth her so by way of eminency, as <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 46. 19. be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause she onely was his wife by design and choice, whereas <ns0:hi>Leah</ns0:hi> was put upon him by fraud, and might have been refused by him, if he had so pleased, and the other two were given to him by <ns0:hi>Rachel</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Leah.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> bare me two <ns0:hi>sons.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="28">28 And the one went out from me, and I said, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 37. 33.</ns0:note> surely he is torn in pieces: and I saw him not since.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="29">29 And if ye take this also from me and mis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />chief befall him, ye shall bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to the grave.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="30">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:42" />30 Now therefore when I come to thy servant my father, and the lad <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> not with us; (seeing that his life is bound up in the lads life)<ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">The death of the Child, which upon this occasion he will firmly believe, will unavoidably procure his death also.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="31">31 It shall come to pass when he seeth that the lad <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> not with us, that he will die, and thy ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vants shall bring down the gray hairs of thy ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vant our father with sorrow to the grave.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="32">32 For thy servant became surety for the lad unto my father, saying, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 43. 9.</ns0:note> If I bring him not unto thee, then I shall bear the blame to my father for ever.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="33">33 Now therefore, I pray thee, let thy ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vant abide in stead of the lad<ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Partly in compassion to our aged father; and partly for thy own advantage; because I can be more serviceable to thee than he because of my greater strength and experience.</ns0:note>, a bondman to my Lord, and let the lad go up with his brethren.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="34">34 For how shall I go up to my father, and the lad be not with me, lest peradventure I see the evil that shall <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> find my father.</ns0:note> come on my father.</ns0:p>
